1csbqu: This week you review two classes that make your stories more fluent. The first teaches you not to repeat nouns without losing clarity; the second, to tell an anecdote with rhythm and to react when someone tells you one. You are joined by Camila, an engineer from Santiago who came back from a conference in Lima… with a suitcase that wasn’t hers.
hukiju: The noun you don’t repeat: “la gris”, “la de Tomás”, “la que…”
obur1o: When everyone knows what you’re talking about, you can drop the noun and keep the article with whatever describes it. The article agrees with the missing noun: “Tengo dos maletas: la gris es mía y la azul, de mi hermana”. It works with an adjective (“la grande”), with “de” + something (“la de Tomás”, “la de las ruedas rotas”) and with “que” + clause (“la que tiene una cinta roja”).
10unz4b: Without a noun, the short possessive (“mi”, “tu”, “su”) doesn’t work: you need the long form with an article: “el mío”, “la tuya”, “los suyos”, “las nuestras”. Since “el suyo” can be his, hers, yours (formal) or theirs, if there’s any doubt use “el de” + person: “el de Camila”, “el de ustedes”.
1d1aewv: Only drop the noun if the reader knows what you mean: if there are two candidates, add “de” + person or a clause with “que”.
hc59v3: Without a noun, the possessive is the long form with an article.
1qhmdjr: With “de” or “que”, you use the article, not “esa”.
7io0yh: Explaining or selecting: apposition and modifier
to81ok: An appositive explains who someone is or what something already identified is; it goes between commas and, if you remove it, the sentence still works: “Tomás, mi compañero de oficina, me llevó al aeropuerto”. It lets you introduce someone without writing another sentence.
17y4a9: A modifier, on the other hand, picks one out of several and goes without commas: “El compañero que vive en Ñuñoa me llevó al aeropuerto” (not the other one). That’s why commas change the meaning: “Los pasajeros, que tenían maletas grandes, esperaron una hora” (all of them) versus “Los pasajeros que tenían maletas grandes esperaron una hora” (only those).

1l8xowb: Telling an anecdote: opening, moving forward and surprising
13zy2o3: An anecdote usually starts with a hook: “¿A que no sabes qué me pasó?”, “Resulta que…”, “Una vez…”. Then you paint the scene in the imperfect or with “estaba” + gerund (“Estaba esperando la maleta y había muchísima gente”) and move forward with the events in the preterite, ordered with “al principio”, “entonces”, “luego”, “al rato” or “a los diez minutos”.
kujw6h: The surprise comes in with “de repente”, “de pronto”, “en ese momento” or “justo cuando” + preterite: “De repente vi una maleta igual que la mía”. For what had happened before, use the pluperfect: “Cuando llegué a la cinta, el señor ya se había llevado la mía”.
64pypp: The background scene with “mientras” goes in the imperfect.
1uncg2i: A sudden event goes in the preterite.
18iep9e: An interrupted action takes “estaba” + gerund; “estuve” presents a closed period (“estuve dos horas esperando”).
1xwy5q1: To close, use “al final” (what happened at the end), “por fin” (something you were waiting for that finally came), “total, que…” (informal summary) and “menos mal que” + indicative (relief): “Menos mal que tenía la etiqueta con mi teléfono”. Don’t use “por fin” for something bad: “Al final perdí el vuelo”, not “por fin perdí el vuelo”.
1aufa1o: The listener has work to do too: “¡No me digas!”, “¿Y entonces?”, “¡Qué mala suerte!”, “¡Menos mal!”, “¡Qué barbaridad!”. “¡Qué fuerte!” is very common in Spain and less so in the Americas. And remember: “darse cuenta de que”, with “de”.

112mtjg: The intonation of a story: keeping the listener waiting
1rvkaba: When you tell an anecdote, not all sentences end the same way. If the story continues, the voice stays suspended at mid-height or rises a little at the end (“Estaba esperando la maleta…”), and the listener knows something more is coming. When you finish a part or the story, the voice clearly falls (“…y era la de otro señor”).
90k8w1: Before the key moment, many speakers make a short pause and stretch the marker a little: “Y de repeeente…”. Appositives between commas are said in a lower tone and a bit faster, like a parenthesis: “Tomás, mi compañero de oficina, me llamó”.
gvn7sq: In writing, appositives and relative clauses that explain go between commas; those that select go without commas. Ellipsis dots (“…”) mark the suspense of the voice in writing.

o5x557: A Chilean blog publishes an anecdote sent in by its readers every week. This one was written by Ignacio, a student from Temuco.
i80ryq: Once, in my first year at university, I travelled to Santiago for a national team match with two friends from school, Matías and Benja. The three of us had almost identical red backpacks: mine had a key ring from La U, Matías’s was a bit torn and Benja’s, since he’s always been the tidiest one, had his name embroidered on it.
10xrtp5: It turns out that after the match we got on a bus full of fans. While we were standing, squashed like sardines, someone started singing and the whole bus began jumping. At that moment the backpacks fell on the floor and got mixed up with other passengers’ bags. A while later we got off, each with a red backpack, and went to the hostel without looking.
t1m41f: That night, when I opened mine, I realised it wasn’t mine: inside there was a nurse’s uniform, a recipe book and an avocado sandwich. Matías had his own, but Benja had a lady’s who, according to the card inside, lived in Maipú. What a pain! My backpack, with my wallet, had disappeared.
15xffn2: Luckily the lady, a very friendly nurse, found my ID card in the pocket and called me the next day. In the end we met at a metro station and swapped backpacks. Since then, mine has a yellow ribbon.
